content: The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) is a fundamental theorem in probability theory that explains the long-term stability of a random variable. When a sample consists of independent and identically distributed random variables with a finite population mean and variance, the average of these observations will eventually converge to and remain close to the population mean. To illustrate this concept, consider rolling a fair six-sided die. The outcomes of such rolls follow a multinomial distribution, where each number (1 through 6) is equally likely to occur. The population mean, or expected value, of these outcomes is calculated as the average of the numbers 1 through 6. In an experiment involving repeated rolls of the die, the average of the outcomes may initially fluctuate significantly. However, as the number of rolls increases, the average will stabilize and approach the true population mean of 3.5. The LLN also applies to proportions. For example, in the case of flipping a fair coin repeatedly, the frequency of heads (or tails) will approach 50% as the number of flips becomes very large. However, the absolute difference between the number of heads and tails may not necessarily decrease. For instance, after 1,000 flips, there might be 520 heads, and after 10,000 flips, there might be 5,096 heads. While the absolute difference has increased from 20 to 96, the proportion of heads has moved closer to the true value of 50%. The LLN is significant because it ensures stable long-term results for random events. For example, in gambling, a casino can expect to retain a consistent percentage of all money wagered (e.g., 3%) over thousands of spins or games. Any temporary winning streaks by players will eventually be outweighed by the statistical parameters of the game. It is crucial to note that the LLN only applies when a large number of observations are considered. There is no guarantee that a small number of observations will converge to the expected value, nor that a streak of one outcome will be immediately balanced by others. This misunderstanding is known as the Gambler’s Fallacy. Historically, Jacob Bernoulli was the first to describe the LLN, remarking that it was so intuitive that even the simplest person instinctively recognizes its truth. Despite this, it took him over 20 years to develop a rigorous mathematical proof, which he published in 1713 in his work Ars Conjectandi (The Art of Conjecturing). He referred to it as his Golden Theorem, but it later became widely known as Bernoulli's Theorem (not to be confused with the physical law of the same name). Later, Siméon Denis Poisson expanded on Bernoulli’s work and introduced the term La loi des grands nombres (The Law of Large Numbers). Over time, the term Law of Large Numbers became the most commonly used name. After Bernoulli and Poisson, other mathematicians, including Chebyshev, Markov, Borel, Cantelli, and Kolmogorov, contributed to refining the LLN. These efforts led to the development of two prominent forms of the LLN: the weak law and the strong law. These are not different laws but rather distinct ways of describing the convergence of observed probabilities to the true probability. The strong form implies the weak form. The Weak Law of Large Numbers The weak law of large numbers states that the sample average converges in probability to the expected value. In other words, for any positive number ε, the probability that the sample average deviates from the expected value by more than ε approaches zero as the sample size increases. This means that the average of many observations will eventually be close to the mean within any specified nonzero margin, no matter how small. This version is called the weak law because convergence in probability is considered a weaker form of convergence for random variables. A consequence of the weak LLN is the asymptotic equipartition property. The Strong Law of Large Numbers The strong law of large numbers states that the sample average converges almost surely to the expected value. This means that, with probability 1, the sample average will eventually equal the expected value as the number of observations approaches infinity. The proof of the strong law is more complex than that of the weak law. This law justifies the intuitive interpretation of the expected value of a random variable as the long-term average when sampling repeatedly. It is called the strong law because almost sure convergence is a stronger form of convergence for random variables. The strong law implies the weak law. In both forms, the LLN holds even if the variance of the random variable is large or infinite, although convergence may be slower in such cases. The assumption of finite variance is often used because it simplifies the mathematical proofs. The distinction between the strong and weak versions lies in the type of convergence being discussed.
